title: Temporal-Access Resource Theory for Continuous Process Tensors
abstract: The uncontrolled endpoint channel can conceal how well a quantum process can protect a logical task under time-resolved control. We formulate a fixed-task resource theory of continuous process tensors with physical access interfaces, entrance-erasing free objects, and budgeted free conversions. Complete-record total-variation error measures performance; the calibrated capability is monotone under conversions that preserve a common free baseline. For unknown-state transmission the baseline is exactly $1-d^{-2}$. Two qubit processes with the same endpoint channel have optimal errors $0$ and $p=\sin^2(2gh)$ at the same finite pulse budget in an ideal-transparent system-only window architecture, forcing any endpoint-only predictor to err by at least $p/2$ on one of them. An exactly solvable family shows how the allocation of a fixed interaction phase around a control window sets the attainable error, and a nontrivial perfect echo requires and attains total control action $π$ in that architecture. The separation extends directly to every qubit unitary target at a budget that includes its boundary gate, while unitary tasks in any dimension have baseline $1-d^{-2}$ whenever a budget-feasible free realization gives the depolarizing output. Complete-record implementation bounds quantify coherent and dissipative control imperfections. Continuous-process randomized compilation supplies physical instrument pullbacks; compatible completion conditions extend their action, and certified dynamical bounds yield achievable task-error and capability guarantees. The resulting theory identifies temporal structure and control investment that endpoint characterization alone cannot resolve.
summary: This work introduces a resource theory for continuous quantum processes that quantifies task protection under time-resolved control. It shows that simply measuring the input and output endpoints is insufficient to characterize the true capability of a quantum process. The theory provides measurable bounds that account for the internal temporal structure and control investment required for a task.
main_problem: The paper develops a fixed-task resource theory for continuous process tensors to quantify how well a quantum process can protect a logical task under time-resolved control, addressing limitations of endpoint-only characterization.
main_result: The theory establishes that internal time controls provide task capabilities that cannot be determined solely by measuring the uncontrolled input-output endpoint channel.
method: It uses operational distance measures based on complete experimental records and defines task error relative to an ideal, resource-rich reference task.
model_or_system: The model involves continuous process tensors (cPTs) describing quantum processes with physical access interfaces, entrance-erasing free objects, and budgeted free conversions.
key_observables: Task error ($\epsilon_	au$), calibrated capability, operational distance ($d_a$), and resource advantage.
important_parameters: Control budget ($B$), time resolution ($\delta t$), and the structure of the physical access interfaces.
main_assumptions: The theory relies on the assumption that the task requires protecting the internal process structure, not just the endpoints, and uses the complete-record convention.
figures_summary: Not specified (Notes refer to TABLE I listing principal symbols and access classes).
paper_structure: The paper builds the theory by defining operational distances and task errors, establishing the free baseline, and then proving separations between endpoint-only characterization and full temporal control capability.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous framework for quantifying control imperfections in open quantum systems by distinguishing between what can be inferred from simple measurements versus what is achievable through active, time-dependent control.
